newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 25.

text.p: The following are the highlights of stories in the Irish press on Tuesday.
- Irish businessman Ben Dunne on Monday handed over a "significant" document to a judge carrying out an inquiry into the payments-to-politicians controversy.
- A passenger whose "illness" forced a flight diversion to Shannon vomited 21 packets of cocaine on Monday and told Irish police he has 11 more still in his stomach.
- Triple Olympic gold medalist Michelle Smith is suing at least four newspapers, a spokesman said on Monday night.
- Ireland cannot join an EU scheme to end systematic internal passport controls because the UK refuses to participate, it emerged last night.

- Trade unions at Telecom Eireann have been given the go-ahead by Communications Minister Alan Dukes to enter into negotiations with management about acquiring a possible 15 percent shareholding in the company for their members.
- Ireland's most senior diplomat in the sphere of Anglo-Irish relations, Sean OhUiginn, is expected to be approved on Tuesday as Ireland's ambassador to the United States.
- Ireland may be advised to stop slaughtering thousands of healthy cattle from farms where a case of BSE has been found.

- The Republican movement should stop blaming the British government and face its responsibility to rebuild the peace process and restore trust, the opposition Fianna Fail leader, Bertie Ahern said on Monday night.
- The Irish government has insisted there will be no further amendments to the proposed 48-hour working week.
- Trades union leaders are to seek an urgent meeting with the opposition Fianna Fail leader, Bertie Ahern, to ask him withdraw his party's opposition to the Working Time Bill.
- The former Fianna Fail politician who it is believed received 1.1 million Irish pounds from Irish businessman Ben Dunne may be identified.

- The Irish pound is expected to strengthen further over the coming weeks but by the end of the year it should be closer to parity with sterling and have lost its edge on its ERM partners, according to a leading Irish economist.

- The Irish Central bank's annual monetary policy statement out today, which is expected to voice concern about rising house prices and the threat of inflation, will have a key influence on short term interest rates and the strength of the Irish pound.
